title: The Whole Earth Catalog — "access to tools"
summary: The 1968 founding catalog itself: a reviewed, reader-contributed index of the best tools, books and skills for self-sufficiency, framed as direct access rather than expert mediation.
how_it_works: Stewart Brand and the POINT Foundation assembled an evaluation-and-access device: each entry reviewed a tool or book, said what it was good for and where to get it, and invited readers to send in their own finds. The editorial focus was self-sufficiency, ecology, alternative education and 'do it yourself' — equipping individuals to shape their own environment instead of depending on institutions.
problem: Ordinary people had no curated, trustworthy way to find the tools and knowledge needed to do things themselves rather than buy finished products or hire experts.
fabcity_relevance: The original 'access to tools' thesis is the direct ancestor of the fab lab idea — that giving people the means of production locally is itself the intervention.

title: The Last Whole Earth Catalog
summary: The 1971 cumulative edition that pulled the project's tool-and-book reviews into a single thick reference, the version that reached the widest audience.
how_it_works: It consolidated years of reviews across shelter, land use, craft, nomadics, communications and 'learning' into one volume, each item still judged by usefulness and accompanied by where to obtain it. As a single object it functioned as a portable library of self-reliance for a generation.
problem: The scattered, frequently-updated catalog needed a durable single edition people could keep and use as a reference.
fabcity_relevance: A single, curated reference of 'what works and where to get it' is exactly the form a fab city repository should aspire to — opinionated, usable, and pointing to real sources.

title: Domebook — build your own geodesic shelter
summary: A hands-on construction manual for building geodesic and zome dwellings, born from the Pacific High School dome-building experiments.
how_it_works: Domebook documented real attempts at building lightweight dome housing — strut and hub geometry, skin and weatherproofing — with the failures included, so readers could put up their own structures cheaply. It treated housing as something a group could fabricate themselves rather than purchase finished.
problem: Conventional housing was expensive and outside individual control; people wanted to build their own efficient shelter.
fabcity_relevance: Open, failure-inclusive build documentation for shelter is the kind of replicable housing knowledge a distributed fabrication network can localize and improve.

title: Energy Primer: Solar, Water, Wind and Biofuels
summary: A 1974 practical survey of renewable energy — solar, water, wind and biofuels — aimed at people wanting to build and run their own systems.
how_it_works: The Primer reviewed renewable-energy methods and the hardware behind them (collectors, wind machines, methane digesters, water power), with enough technical grounding and sources for readers to design small-scale systems. It framed energy as something a household or community could produce, not only consume.
problem: Households and communities had no accessible, trustworthy guide to building their own renewable energy systems.
fabcity_relevance: A buildable renewable-energy reference is core infrastructure for a locally-productive city aiming to make its own energy 'you can touch.'

title: Soft-Tech — appropriate technology compendium
summary: A 1978 collection (from CoEvolution Quarterly) of 'soft' or appropriate technologies: small-scale, low-impact, locally-repairable systems.
how_it_works: Soft-Tech gathered articles and reviews on decentralized, human-scale technology — energy, building, water, waste — favouring systems people could understand, build and fix themselves over large centralized infrastructure. It argued the politics of a technology is inseparable from its scale and repairability.
problem: Centralized, high-tech infrastructure left people unable to understand, build or repair the systems they depended on.
fabcity_relevance: The 'appropriate technology' argument — human-scale, understandable, repairable — is the intellectual bridge between Whole Earth and the technological-disobedience and fab-city positions.

title: The Whole Earth Ecolog — environmental tools
summary: The 1990 environmentally-focused edition of the catalog, reviewing the best tools, books and practices for ecological restoration and living.
how_it_works: The Ecolog applied the catalog method specifically to ecology — soil, water, habitat, pollution, restoration — reviewing what to read, what to use and who to learn from for people wanting to act on environmental problems directly.
problem: People wanting to take ecological action lacked a curated guide to the tools, books and practices that actually help.
fabcity_relevance: A curated, action-oriented environmental toolset is the kind of practice-library a fab city can localize to its own bioregion.
